steps.title: Prosecco DOC
steps.body: Glera grows mainly in the Veneto and Friuli-Venezia Giulia, in north-east Italy. Prosecco DOC covers a large area across nine provinces and must be at least 85% Glera. It's mostly flat land, giving large volumes of fresh, affordable wine. Prosecco Rosé, with Pinot Noir, was allowed from 2020.

steps.title: Tank method
steps.body: Most Prosecco is made by the tank method, also called Martinotti or Charmat: the second fermentation happens in large pressurised tanks, often over a few weeks. This keeps Glera's fresh fruit and floral aromas, without the bready notes of long lees ageing. It's also faster and cheaper than the traditional method.

steps.prompt: Match each Prosecco term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Prosecco has its own rules and words.

steps.title: Sweetness
steps.body: Prosecco is labelled by sweetness: Brut, up to 12 g/l; Extra Dry, 12 to 17 g/l; Dry, 17 to 32 g/l. Confusingly, Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut. Extra Dry is the traditional style, with a soft touch of sweetness balancing the acidity.
steps.highlight: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut

steps.prompt: Which Prosecco is sweeter: Brut or Extra Dry?
steps.explanation: Extra Dry has 12 to 17 g/l; Brut up to 12.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prosecco DOC covers nine provinces, at least 85% Glera
The tank method keeps Glera's fruit fresh
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut
